claim: When the eyes view separate and incompatible images, the brain suppresses one image and promotes the other into visual awareness.
source: When the eyes view separate and incompatible images, the brain suppresses one image and promotes the other into visual awareness.
evidence: This is a well-established phenomenon in vision science, drawing from established scientific consensus about binocular rivalry and interocular suppression.

claim: Periods of interocular suppression can be prolonged during continuous flash suppression (CFS) when one eye views a static 'target' while the other views a complex dynamic stimulus.
source: Periods of interocular suppression can be prolonged during continuous flash suppression (CFS) – when one eye views a static 'target' while the other views a complex dynamic stimulus.
evidence: This describes the established CFS paradigm, drawing from scientific knowledge about the technique.

claim: Measuring the time needed for a suppressed image to break CFS (bCFS) has been widely used to investigate unconscious processing.
source: Measuring the time needed for a suppressed image to break CFS (bCFS) has been widely used to investigate unconscious processing, and the results have generated controversy regarding the scope of visual processing without awareness.
evidence: This statement references the widespread use of bCFS methodology in the field, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: bCFS results have generated controversy regarding the scope of visual processing without awareness.
source: Measuring the time needed for a suppressed image to break CFS (bCFS) has been widely used to investigate unconscious processing, and the results have generated controversy regarding the scope of visual processing without awareness.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations in the Introduction discussing controversies in the field.

claim: tCFS provides a measure of suppression depth by quantifying the difference between breakthrough and suppression thresholds.
source: Unlike bCFS, tCFS provides a measure of suppression depth by quantifying the difference between breakthrough and suppression thresholds.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the new tCFS paradigm introduced in this study, supported by the experimental design and data presented.

claim: Breakthrough thresholds differ across target types (e.g. faces vs gratings).
source: tCFS confirms that (i) breakthrough thresholds indeed differ across target types (e.g. faces vs gratings, as bCFS has shown)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2 showing differences in bCFS thresholds across image categories.

claim: Suppression depth does not vary across target types.
source: tCFS confirms that (i) breakthrough thresholds indeed differ across target types (e.g. faces vs gratings, as bCFS has shown) – but (ii) suppression depth does not vary across target types.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data from Experiments 1 and 2 showing uniform suppression depth across image categories.

claim: All stimuli require a strikingly uniform reduction in contrast to reach the corresponding suppression threshold once the breakthrough contrast is reached.
source: Once the breakthrough contrast is reached for a given stimulus, all stimuli require a strikingly uniform reduction in contrast to reach the corresponding suppression threshold.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing approximately 15 dB suppression depth across all image categories in Experiment 2.

claim: Uniform suppression depth points to a single mechanism of CFS suppression.
source: This uniform suppression depth points to a single mechanism of CFS suppression, one that likely occurs early in visual processing because suppression depth was not modulated by target salience or complexity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the uniform suppression depth data across different image types.

claim: The CFS suppression mechanism likely occurs early in visual processing because suppression depth was not modulated by target salience or complexity.
source: This uniform suppression depth points to a single mechanism of CFS suppression, one that likely occurs early in visual processing because suppression depth was not modulated by target salience or complexity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that suppression depth was uniform across image types varying in complexity and salience.

claim: Variations in bCFS thresholds alone are insufficient for inferring whether the barrier to achieving awareness exerted by interocular suppression is weaker for some categories of visual stimuli compared to others.
source: More fundamentally, it shows that variations in bCFS thresholds alone are insufficient for inferring whether the barrier to achieving awareness exerted by interocular suppression is weaker for some categories of visual stimuli compared to others.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the finding that while bCFS thresholds vary, suppression depth remains constant across image categories.

claim: There are controversial claims of higher level semantic processing occurring outside of awareness.
source: There are controversial claims of higher level semantic processing (Lanfranco et al., 2023; Mudrik et al., 2014; Stein and Sterzer, 2014; Sterzer et al., 2014), object categorization (Kouider and Dehaene, 2007; Rees, 2007; Sterzer et al., 2014), and abstract reasoning (Hassin, 2013; Sklar et al., 2012) occurring outside of awareness.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies making such claims.

claim: Binocular rivalry and continuous flash suppression are two of the most popular methods for manipulating visual awareness in recent years.
source: A number of methods exist for manipulating visual awareness (Kim and Blake, 2005), with two of the most popular in recent years being binocular rivalry (Alais and Blake, 2014) and continuous flash suppression (CFS: Fang and He, 2005; Tsuchiya and Koch, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature and reflects established knowledge in the field.

claim: Both binocular rivalry and CFS rely on interocular suppression induced by dissimilar monocular images independently presented to each eye.
source: Both rely on interocular suppression induced by dissimilar monocular images independently presented to each eye, the result being that only one eye's image is perceived (i.e. dominates) at any given moment, with the other suppressed from awareness.
evidence: This describes the established mechanisms of these techniques, drawing from scientific knowledge.

claim: In binocular rivalry with images approximately matched in salience, monocular suppression lasts for just a few seconds before switching to suppress the other eye.
source: For images approximately matched in salience, as often is the case in binocular rivalry (Alais and Blake, 2014; Wang et al., 2023), monocular suppression lasts for just a few seconds before switching to suppress the other eye (and so on, alternating irregularly over time).
evidence: This is supported by citations to binocular rivalry literature and reflects established knowledge about the phenomenon.

claim: With CFS, a highly salient stream of dynamic images seen by one eye suppresses a smaller, weaker target presented to the other for considerably longer periods of suppression that can last tens of seconds.
source: With CFS, a highly salient stream of dynamic images seen by one eye suppresses a smaller, weaker target presented to the other for considerably longer periods of suppression that can last tens of seconds.
evidence: This describes the established characteristics of CFS, drawing from scientific knowledge about the technique.

claim: The breaking CFS (bCFS) variant was introduced by Jiang et al., 2007.
source: A commonly used variant known as 'breaking CFS' (bCFS) was introduced by Jiang et al., 2007 in which the suppressed target slowly ramps up from low contrast until it becomes sufficiently strong to break suppression and achieve visibility.
evidence: This is supported by a direct citation to the original study.

claim: In bCFS, the suppressed target slowly ramps up from low contrast until it becomes sufficiently strong to break suppression and achieve visibility.
source: A commonly used variant known as 'breaking CFS' (bCFS) was introduced by Jiang et al., 2007 in which the suppressed target slowly ramps up from low contrast until it becomes sufficiently strong to break suppression and achieve visibility.
evidence: This describes the established bCFS methodology, supported by citation and knowledge.

claim: Differences in breakthrough times among various image types have been used to support claims for unconscious processing of certain visual images.
source: Time to breakthrough has become a popular measure, and differences in breakthrough times among various image types have been used to support claims for unconscious processing of certain visual images.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations throughout the manuscript to studies making such claims.

claim: Image types that consistently emerge from suppression more rapidly than other image types are construed to be ones that receive prioritized processing outside of awareness.
source: According to this line of reasoning, image types that consistently emerge from suppression more rapidly than do other image types are construed to be ones that receive prioritized processing outside of awareness.
evidence: This describes the reasoning used in previous bCFS studies, supported by citations.

claim: Faces portraying emotional expressions break suppression faster than neutral faces.
source: To give three examples of this purported effect, faces portraying emotional expressions break suppression faster than do neutral faces (Alais, 2012; Jiang et al., 2007; Tsuchiya et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies reporting this effect.

claim: Complex scenes containing incongruent objects break suppression faster than congruent scenes.
source: complex scenes containing incongruent objects break suppression faster than do congruent scenes (Mudrik et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study reporting this effect.

claim: Native words break suppression faster than unfamiliar foreign words.
source: native words break suppression faster than do unfamiliar foreign words (Jiang et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study reporting this effect.

claim: Sceptics argue that differences in breakthrough times can be attributed to low-level factors such as spatial frequency, orientation and contrast that vary between images.
source: Sceptics argue, however, that differences in breakthrough times can be attributed to low-level factors such as spatial frequency, orientation and contrast that vary between images (Gayet et al., 2014; Moors and Hesselmann, 2018; Moors et al., 2016; Moors et al., 2017; Moors & Hesselmann, 2018; Stuit et al., 2023)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies making this argument.

claim: Breakthrough times alone are insufficient to measure differential unconscious processing.
source: and more fundamentally, that breakthrough times alone are insufficient to measure differential unconscious processing (Stein and Hesselmann, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study making this argument.

claim: Conclusions based on a comparison of bCFS breakthrough times between different image categories suffer from a problem of unidirectionality and a false assumption of image equivalence.
source: Conclusions based on a comparison of bCFS breakthrough times between different image categories suffer from a problem of unidirectionality and a false assumption of image equivalence
evidence: This is an inference and argument made by the authors based on their analysis of the literature.

claim: Images producing faster breakthrough times are interpreted as undergoing residual processing outside of awareness, adding to their salience and weakening their interocular suppression.
source: Images producing faster breakthrough times (equivalently, lower breakthrough contrasts) are interpreted as undergoing residual processing outside of awareness, adding to their salience and weakening their interocular suppression (Mudrik et al., 2011; Sterzer et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2010b; Zhou et al., 2010a).
evidence: This describes the interpretation used in previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: An implicit assumption in bCFS studies is that as all images were initially invisible, the depth of interocular suppression was weaker for images that break suppression more quickly.
source: An implicit assumption here is that as all images were initially invisible, the depth of interocular suppression was thus weaker for images that break suppression more quickly (i.e. produce faster reaction times, as sometimes stated).
evidence: This is an inference about the assumptions underlying previous bCFS studies.

claim: The depth of interocular suppression is rarely measured in CFS paradigms.
source: Yet, the depth of interocular suppression is rarely measured in CFS paradigms (see Tsuchiya et al., 2006 for an exception)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to one exception and reflects the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Suppression depth has not been explicitly compared between image categories in CFS studies.
source: and to our knowledge, has not been explicitly compared between image categories.
evidence: This reflects the authors' knowledge of the literature and identifies a gap in previous research.

claim: One method for measuring interocular suppression is to compare the threshold for change-detection in a target when it is monocularly suppressed and when it is dominant.
source: One method for measuring interocular suppression is to compare the threshold for change-detection in a target when it is monocularly suppressed and when it is dominant, an established strategy in binocular rivalry research (Alais, 2012; Alais et al., 2010; Alais and Melcher, 2007; Nguyen et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies using this method.

claim: Probe studies using contrast as the dependent variable for thresholds measured during dominance and during suppression can advantageously standardise suppression depth in units of contrast within the same stimulus.
source: Probe studies using contrast as the dependent variable for thresholds measured during dominance and during suppression can advantageously standardise suppression depth in units of contrast within the same stimulus (e.g. Alais and Melcher, 2007; Ling et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies using this approach.

claim: In Experiment 1, there was a significant main effect of threshold, such that bCFS thresholds were significantly higher than reCFS thresholds.
source: A repeated-measures ANOVA revealed a significant main effect of threshold, such that bCFS thresholds were significantly higher than reCFS thresholds (F(1,19) = 50.39, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.73).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, there was a significant interaction between threshold and condition, indicating that the difference between bCFS and reCFS thresholds was influenced by whether they were recorded using the discrete trial procedure or the continuous trial procedure.
source: There was also a significant interaction between threshold and condition (F(1,19) = 41.19, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.68), indicating that the difference between bCFS and reCFS thresholds was influenced by whether they were recorded using the discrete trial procedure or the continuous trial procedure.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, bCFS and reCFS thresholds differed within each type of procedure (discrete and continuous).
source: Subsequent post-hoc tests revealed that bCFS and reCFS thresholds differed within each type of procedure (Discrete: t(19) = 2.89, p=0.009, d=0.65 Continuous: t(19) = 12.12, p<0.001, d=2.7).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, suppression depth was larger with the continuous procedure (M=–15.40 dB, SD = 5.68) compared to the discrete procedure (M=–5.74 dB, SD = 8.89).
source: Overall, the suppression depth (i.e. the difference between bCFS and reCFS thresholds) was larger with the continuous procedure (M=–15.40 dB, SD = 5.68) compared to the discrete procedure (M=–5.74 dB, SD = 8.89), t(19) = 6.42, p<0.001, d=1.3
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, there was no significant effect of image type (face vs object) on suppression depth.
source: We again found significant main effects of threshold (F(1,19) = 50.39, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.73), and a threshold x condition interaction (F(1,19) = 41.19, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.68), but non-significance for the effect of image type (p=0.26).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, Bayesian analysis found that the best model to explain suppression depth included the main effect of procedure (BF10=3231.74), and weak evidence/data insensitivity for image type (BF10=0.37).
source: A Bayesian repeated-measures ANOVA (2x2; procedure x image type on suppression depth) found that the best model to explain suppression depth included the main effect of procedure (BF10=3231.74), and weak evidence/data insensitivity for image type (BF10=0.37).
evidence: This is supported by Bayesian statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 2, there was a significant main effect of threshold (bCFS vs reCFS).
source: A 2x5 repeated-measures ANOVA revealed a significant main effect of threshold (bCFS vs reCFS; F(1,17) = 133.79, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.89), and image type (F(4,68) = 13.45, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.44).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, there was a significant main effect of image type.
source: A 2x5 repeated-measures ANOVA revealed a significant main effect of threshold (bCFS vs reCFS; F(1,17) = 133.79, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.89), and image type (F(4,68) = 13.45, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.44).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, there was no significant interaction between thresholds and image type, indicating that the relationship between bCFS and reCFS thresholds was invariant across image categories.
source: Critically however, there was no significant interaction between thresholds and image type (p=0.98), indicating that the relationship between bCFS and reCFS thresholds was invariant across image categories.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, Bayesian analysis confirmed strong evidence in favor of the null hypothesis for the effect of image categories on suppression depth (BF01 = 20.30).
source: A Bayesian repeated-measures ANOVA (1x5, effect of image categories on suppression depth), confirmed strong evidence in favor of the null hypothesis (BF01 = 20.30).
evidence: This is supported by Bayesian statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, bCFS thresholds differed significantly over image type.
source: which clearly shows differences in bCFS thresholds (blue symbols in Figure 3a) over image type (1x5 repeated-measures ANOVA; F(4,68) = 16.29, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.49)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 2 and shown in Figure 3a.

claim: In Experiment 2, scrambled noise images yield breakthrough thresholds 5.3 dB higher than face images.
source: Scrambled noise images, for example, yield breakthrough thresholds 5.3 dB higher than do face images
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, linear gratings breakthrough thresholds are 3.0 dB higher than polar gratings.
source: and linear gratings breakthrough thresholds are 3.0 dB higher than polar gratings.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, reCFS thresholds exhibit the same pattern of differences over image type as bCFS thresholds.
source: Critically, Figure 3 also shows that reCFS thresholds exhibit the same pattern of differences over image type (red symbols in Figure 3a)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2 shown in Figure 3a.

claim: In Experiment 2, approximately 15 dB of suppression depth was observed.
source: Replicating the result of Experiment 1, approximately 15 dB of suppression depth was observed in Experiment 2 (Figure 3b)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2 shown in Figure 3b.

claim: In Experiment 2, a repeated-measures ANOVA confirmed that suppression depth did not differ across image categories (F(4,68) = 0.1, p=0.98).
source: A repeated-measures ANOVA confirmed that suppression depth did not differ across image categories (F(4,68) = 0.1, p=0.98).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: The uniformity of suppression depth across target image categories in CFS could indicate that neural events mediating CFS suppression transpire within a common visual mechanism, one that is not selective for image type, complexity or semantic meaning.
source: This uniformity of suppression depth could indicate that neural events mediating CFS suppression transpire within a common visual mechanism, one that is not selective for image type, complexity or semantic meaning.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings of uniform suppression depth.

claim: The uniform suppression depth finding is compatible with popular models of binocular rivalry built around the concept of reciprocal inhibition and neural adaptation.
source: This view is compatible with popular models of binocular rivalry built around the concept of reciprocal inhibition and neural adaptation (Alais et al., 2010; Kang and Blake, 2010; Mcdougall, 1901)
evidence: This is an inference connecting the experimental findings to existing theoretical models, supported by citations.

claim: The uniform suppression depth finding is compatible with Bayesian-inspired inference-based models in which perceptual alternations in dominance are triggered by accumulating residual error signal associated with competing stimulus interpretations.
source: as well as with more recent Bayesian-inspired inference-based models in which perceptual alternations in dominance are triggered by accumulating residual error signal associated with competing stimulus interpretations (Hohwy et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the experimental findings to existing theoretical models, supported by a citation.

claim: Steadily increasing error signal effectively plays the same role as steadily decreasing inhibition strength caused by neural adaptation in reciprocal inhibition models.
source: As pointed out elsewhere (Blake, 2022), steadily increasing error signal effectively plays the same role as does steadily decreasing inhibition strength caused by neural adaptation in reciprocal inhibition models.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a theoretical discussion.

claim: The depth of suppression should be positively related to the rate of target change.
source: Expressed in operational terms, the depth of suppression should be positively related to the rate of target change.
evidence: This is a prediction based on theoretical reasoning about adaptation and inhibition models.

claim: In Experiment 3, there was a significant main effect of threshold, indicating that bCFS and reCFS contrasts differ.
source: There was a significant main effect of threshold (F(1,16) = 116.56, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.88) again indicating that bCFS and reCFS contrasts differ.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 3, there was a significant main effect of image type, with no interaction with threshold.
source: There was also a significant main effect of image type (F(3,48) = 9.40, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.37), again with no interaction with threshold (p=0.19).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 3, bCFS and reCFS thresholds vary in tandem regardless of image type.
source: This result indicates that bCFS and reCFS thresholds vary in tandem regardless of image type.
evidence: This is an inference from the statistical analysis showing no interaction between threshold and image type.

claim: In Experiment 3, Bayesian model comparison demonstrated moderate support for the null effect of image category on suppression depth (BF01 = 4.06).
source: This null-effect of image-type was again confirmed with a Bayesian model comparison (3 speed x 4 image categories on suppression depth), demonstrating moderate support for the null effect of image category (BF01 = 4.06).
evidence: This is supported by Bayesian statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 3, there was a significant interaction between rate of contrast change and thresholds, indicating that the difference between bCFS and reCFS thresholds (i.e. suppression depth) depended on the target's rate of contrast change.
source: Critically, there was a significant interaction between rate of contrast change and thresholds (F(2,32) = 128.60, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.89), as expected, indicating that the difference between bCFS and reCFS thresholds (i.e. suppression depth) depended on the target's rate of contrast change.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 3, as the rate of contrast change increases, suppression depth increases (Slow M=9.64 dB, SD = 4.37, Medium M=14.6 dB, SD = 5.43; Fast M=18.97 dB, SD = 6.93).
source: Figure 4 displays a summary of these results (averaged across image types), showing that as the rate of contrast change increases, so does suppression depth (Slow M=9.64 dB, SD = 4.37, Medium M=14.6 dB, SD = 5.43; Fast M=18.97 dB, SD = 6.93).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 3 shown in Figure 4.

claim: In Experiment 3, the distribution of percept durations varied by rate of contrast change, with shorter median percept durations for fast rates of contrast change (M = 3.08, SD = 1.07), and slower percept durations for slow rates of contrast change (M=4.61, SD = 2.05) compared to medium (M = 3.45, SD = 1.29).
source: In Experiment 3, however, the distribution of percept durations is shown to vary by rate of contrast change. With shorter median percept durations for fast rates of contrast change (M = 3.08, SD = 1.07), and slower percept durations for slow rates of contrast change (M=4.61, SD = 2.05) compared to medium (M = 3.45, SD = 1.29).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 3, a repeated measures ANOVA confirmed that median percept durations varied by rate of contrast change (F(2,32) = 30.89, p<0.001, ηp2=0.66).
source: A repeated measures ANOVA confirmed that median percept durations varied by rate of contrast change (F(2,32) = 30.89, p<0.001, ηp2=0.66).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: The differences in suppression depth in Experiment 3 were not driven by fixed rates of perceptual alternation across the three levels of rate of contrast change.
source: This analysis thus confirmed that these differences in suppression depth were not driven by fixed rates of perceptual alternation across the three levels of rate of contrast change (Figure 4c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of percept duration data from Experiment 3.

claim: Sequential changes in suppression depth were well described by the damped harmonic oscillator model of excitation and inhibition.
source: As can be appreciated in Figure 5c, sequential changes in suppression depth were well described by the damped harmonic oscillator model of excitation and inhibition, which well captured the modulations early in the trial.
evidence: This is supported by model fitting analysis shown in Figure 5c.

claim: For each rate of target contrast change, the damped harmonic oscillator model was the superior fit to the data (Slow contrast change, R2=0.68, BIC = –1847.2; Medium contrast change, R2=0.63, BIC = –2125.29; Fast contrast change, R2=0.36, BIC = –1041.29).
source: For each rate of target contrast change, the damped harmonic oscillator model was the superior fit to the data (Slow contrast change, R2=0.68, BIC = –1847.2; Medium contrast change, R2=0.63, BIC = –2125.29; Fast contrast change, R2=0.36, BIC = –1041.29).
evidence: This is supported by model fitting analysis of experimental data.

claim: The change in Bayesian Information Criterion between the damped harmonic oscillator and the next best fitting cubic polynomial model was large for all rates of contrast change (Slow contrast change, ΔBIC = –1072.88; Medium contrast change, ΔBIC = –781.5; Fast contrast change, ΔBIC = –97.06).
source: In each case, the change in Bayesian Information Criterion between the damped harmonic oscillator and the next best fitting cubic polynomial model was large (Slow contrast change, ΔBIC = –1072.88; Medium contrast change, ΔBIC = –781.5; Fast contrast change, ΔBIC = –97.06).
evidence: This is supported by model comparison analysis of experimental data.

claim: The tCFS method offers the advantage of being fast and efficient, with 90 s sufficient to collect a robust set of data comprising 16 thresholds, eight each for bCFS and reCFS.
source: First, it is fast and efficient. The data in Figure 2b, for example, show that 90 s is sufficient to collect a robust set of data comprising 16 thresholds, eight each for bCFS and reCFS.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: By providing easy quantification of breakthrough and suppression thresholds, tCFS allows the calculation of a rational index of strength of suppression for evaluating whether certain categories of images receive prioritized processing.
source: The second advantage is that by providing easy quantification of breakthrough and suppression thresholds, tCFS allows the calculation of a rational index of strength of suppression for evaluating whether certain categories of images (e.g. faces) receive prioritized processing, a controversial issue within the CFS literature.
evidence: This is an inference about the methodological advantages of tCFS based on the experimental design.

claim: The difference between bCFS and reCFS thresholds indicates that suppression is not a passive process where a given contrast threshold determines a narrow awareness/suppression border.
source: For both conditions, significant differences between bCFS and reCFS thresholds were observed. This difference indicates that suppression is not a passive process where a given contrast threshold determines a narrow awareness/suppression border.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental finding of significant differences between bCFS and reCFS thresholds.

claim: There is a contrast range (i.e. suppression depth) between awareness and suppression.
source: Instead, there is a contrast range (i.e. suppression depth) between awareness and suppression.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental finding of significant differences between bCFS and reCFS thresholds.

claim: The finding of suppression depth is consistent with models of interocular suppression involving mutually inhibitory left- and right-eye processes.
source: This is consistent with models of interocular suppression involving mutually inhibitory left- and right-eye processes.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the experimental findings to existing theoretical models.

claim: The fact that binocular rivalry produces a significant degree of suppression depth is well known in that literature but is rarely considered in CFS studies.
source: The fact that binocular rivalry produces a significant degree of suppression depth is well known in that literature (Blake and Camisa, 1979; Nguyen et al., 2003) but is rarely considered in CFS studies (an exception to this rule is the study by Tsuchiya et al., 2006 who used a briefly presented test probe to compare depth of suppression associated with CFS and with BR; suppression depth was considerably larger for the former than for the latter)
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature and reflects knowledge of the field.

claim: In the discrete conditions of Experiment 1, some participants showed an inverse effect where reCFS thresholds were higher than bCFS thresholds (n=4).
source: Intuitively, the average contrast threshold for reCFS should be lower than for bCFS, yet in the discrete conditions there were some participants who showed the inverse effect (n=4; Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 1 shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Saccades, blinks, or other oculomotor reflexes that differentially impact transitions during interocular rivalry might have influenced the discrete bCFS and reCFS trials at separate times.
source: One possibility is that saccades, blinks, or other oculomotor reflexes that differentially impact transitions during interocular rivalry (van Dam and van Ee, 2006a; van Dam and van Ee, 2006b) might have influenced the discrete bCFS and reCFS trials at separate times.
evidence: This is speculation about possible explanations for the inverse effect observed in some participants, supported by citations.

claim: In the tCFS procedure, no participant showed an inverse effect where reCFS thresholds were higher than bCFS thresholds.
source: These possibilities highlight inherent advantages and controls of the tCFS procedure, for which no participant showed an inverse effect
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the tCFS conditions.

claim: The existence of distinctly different, complementary transition thresholds for bCFS and reCFS is reminiscent of the behavior termed hysteresis.
source: As an aside, the existence of distinctly different, complementary transition thresholds for bCFS and reCFS is reminiscent of the behavior termed hysteresis: a property of dynamical systems wherein output values, rather than being solely governed by corresponding input values, also exhibit lags or delays based on the valence of continuous changes in the input values.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the experimental findings to the concept of hysteresis from dynamical systems theory.

claim: Examples of hysteresis in visual perception include transitions between binocular fusion and binocular rivalry, perception of motion direction in random-dot cinematograms, and repetition priming in perception of bistable configurations.
source: Examples of hysteresis in visual perception include transitions between binocular fusion and binocular rivalry (Anderson, 1992; Buckthought et al., 2008; Julesz and Tyler, 1976), perception of motion direction in random-dot cinematograms (Williams et al., 1986), and repetition priming in perception of bistable configurations (Pastukhov et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies demonstrating hysteresis in various visual phenomena.

claim: Hysteresis can be construed as a form of memory whereby prior states influence the persistence of current states into the future.
source: To paraphrase Maglio and Polman, 2016, hysteresis can be construed as a form of memory whereby prior states influence the persistence of current states into the future.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a theoretical discussion of hysteresis.

claim: A number of previous studies have interpreted differences in bCFS thresholds (or suppression durations) for different categories of images without taking into account thresholds for inducing suppression.
source: As noted in the Introduction, a number of previous studies have interpreted differences in bCFS thresholds (or suppression durations) for different categories of images without taking into account thresholds for inducing suppression, which we believe is an important piece of information necessary for calculating suppression depth.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of previous research based on the authors' analysis of the literature.

claim: The failure to obtain evidence for category specific suppression depth could be argued to be based on the limited range of image categories sampled in this study.
source: Nevertheless, one could argue that our failure to obtain evidence for category specific suppression depth is based on the limited range of image categories sampled in this study.
evidence: This is speculation about a potential limitation of the study.

claim: It would be informative to broaden the range of image types tested using tCFS to include images varying in familiarity, congruence and affect.
source: We agree it would be informative to broaden the range of image types tested using tCFS to include images varying in familiarity, congruence and affect.
evidence: This is speculation about future research directions.

claim: Dynamic configurations of small dots varying in location over time can create the compelling impression of rotational motion of a rigid, 3D object (structure from motion) or of a human engaged in given activity (biological motion).
source: To give a few examples, dynamic configurations of small dots varying in location over time can create the compelling impression of rotational motion of a rigid, 3D object (structure from motion) or of a human engaged in given activity (biological motion) (Grossmann and Dobbins, 2006; Watson et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies demonstrating these perceptual phenomena.

claim: Structure from motion and biological motion stimuli are associated with neural processing in higher-tier visual areas of the human brain, including the superior occipital lateral region and the posterior portion of the superior temporal sulcus.
source: These kinds of visual stimuli are associated with neural processing in higher-tier visual areas of the human brain, including the superior occipital lateral region (e.g. Vanduffel et al., 2002) and the posterior portion of the superior temporal sulcus (e.g. Grossman et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to neuroimaging studies.

claim: Zhou et al., 2021 found that genuine face images and faux faces remained suppressed for equivalent durations whereas genuine faces remained dominant significantly longer than did faux faces.
source: In their study, genuine face images and faux faces remained suppressed for equivalent durations whereas genuine faces remained dominant significantly longer than did faux faces.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: If a certain image type had overall lower bCFS and reCFS contrast thresholds relative to another image type (despite equivalent suppression depth), this would not necessarily imply the former image enjoyed 'preferential processing' relative to the latter.
source: Next, we turn to another question raised about our conclusion concerning invariant depth of suppression. If a certain image type had overall lower bCFS and reCFS contrast thresholds relative to another image type (despite equivalent suppression depth), would that imply the former image enjoyed 'preferential processing' relative to the latter?
evidence: This is an inference about the interpretation of the results, posed as a rhetorical question.

claim: Polar patterns tend to emerge from suppression at slightly lower contrasts than gratings.
source: Figure 3 shows that polar patterns tend to emerge from suppression at slightly lower contrasts than do gratings
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Polar patterns, once dominant, tend to maintain dominance to lower contrasts than gratings.
source: and that polar patterns, once dominant, tend to maintain dominance to lower contrasts than do gratings
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: Neural responses to changing contrast will depend on the neural contrast response functions (CRFs) of the cells responding to each type of stimulus.
source: But while rate of contrast change is identical, the neural responses to those contrast changes may not be the same: neural responses to changing contrast will depend on the neural contrast response functions (CRFs) of the cells responding to each of those two types of stimuli, where the CRF defines the relationship between neural response and stimulus contrast.
evidence: This draws from established knowledge about neural contrast response functions.

claim: CRFs rise monotonically with contrast and typically exhibit a steeply rising initial response as stimulus contrast rises from low to moderate values, followed by a reduced growth rate for higher contrasts.
source: CRFs rise monotonically with contrast and typically exhibit a steeply rising initial response as stimulus contrast rises from low to moderate values, followed by a reduced growth rate for higher contrasts.
evidence: This draws from established knowledge about neural contrast response functions.

claim: CRFs for neurons in mid-level vision areas such as V4 and FFA are generally steeper and shifted toward lower contrasts than CRFs for neurons in primary visual cortex.
source: CRFs for neurons in mid-level vision areas such as V4 and FFA (which respond well to polar stimuli and faces, respectively) are generally steeper and shifted toward lower contrasts than CRFs for neurons in primary visual cortex (which respond well to gratings).
evidence: This draws from established knowledge about neural contrast response functions in different visual areas.

claim: The effective strength of the contrast changes in the tCFS procedure will depend on the shape and position of the underlying CRF.
source: Therefore, the effective strength of the contrast changes in our tCFS procedure will depend on the shape and position of the underlying CRF, an idea we develop in more detail in Appendix 1, comparing the case of V1 and V4 CRFs.
evidence: This is an inference about how CRFs might influence tCFS results.

claim: The comparison of V1 and V4 CRFs shows that V4 CRFs should produce much lower bCFS and reCFS thresholds than V1 CRFs, and that V4 CRFs should produce much more suppression than V1 CRFs.
source: Interestingly, the comparison of V1 and V4 CRFs shows two interesting points: (i) that V4 CRFs should produce much lower bCFS and reCFS thresholds than V1 CRFs, and (ii) that V4 CRFs should produce much more suppression than V1 CRFs.
evidence: This is an inference based on theoretical analysis presented in Appendix 1.

claim: The experimental data do not support the prediction that V4 CRFs should produce much lower bCFS and reCFS thresholds than V1 CRFs or much more suppression.
source: Our data do not support either prediction: bCFS and reCFS thresholds for the polar shape are not 'much lower' than those for gratings (Figure 3) and neither is there 'much more' suppression depth for the polar form.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2 shown in Figure 3.

claim: There is no room in these results to support the claim that certain images are special and receive 'preferential processing' or processing outside of awareness.
source: There is no room in these results to support the claim that certain images are special and receive 'preferential processing' or processing outside of awareness.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The similar data patterns for all image types is most parsimoniously explained by a single mechanism processing all images.
source: Instead, the similar data patterns for all image types is most parsimoniously explained by a single mechanism processing all images (see Appendix 1)
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings based on parsimony.

claim: Blake and Fox, 1974 concluded that rivalry suppression is non-selective based on a task where observers were unable to notice large changes in the spatial frequency or orientation of a suppressed grating.
source: Blake and Fox, 1974 concluded that rivalry suppression is non-selective based on a task where observers were unable to notice large changes in the spatial frequency or orientation of a suppressed grating.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Alais and Melcher, 2007 found that the detectability of a brief, monocular probe presented to an eye during rivalry varied depending on the 'complexity' of the stimulus being probed, with suppression being greater for complex images.
source: On the other hand, Alais and Melcher, 2007 found that the detectability of a brief, monocular probe presented to an eye during rivalry varied depending on the 'complexity' (e.g. grating vs face) of the stimulus being probed, with suppression being greater for complex images.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Tsuchiya et al., 2006 found that detection of a brief test probe was much more difficult to detect when presented to an eye during suppression phases of CFS compared to binocular rivalry.
source: Tsuchiya et al., 2006 found that detection of a brief test probe was much more difficult to detect when presented to an eye during suppression phases of CFS compared to binocular rivalry.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Durations of suppression phases associated with CFS are considerably longer than those associated with rivalry (~15 x longer, in the study by Blake et al., 2019).
source: In a similar vein, durations of suppression phases associated with CFS are considerably longer than those associated with rivalry (~15 x longer, in the study by Blake et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: bCFS thresholds will be slightly overestimated due to the brief reaction time delay between the perceived transition and execution of the motor response signalling that event.
source: Turning to a methodological issue, an important caveat for interpreting suppression depth during tCFS is that bCFS thresholds will be slightly overestimated due to the brief reaction time delay between the perceived transition and execution of the motor response signalling that event (a problem for most bCFS studies).
evidence: This is an inference about a methodological limitation based on knowledge of reaction time delays.

claim: reCFS thresholds will be slightly underestimated because of the response delay.
source: By the same token, reCFS thresholds will be slightly underestimated because of this response delay.
evidence: This is an inference about a methodological limitation based on knowledge of reaction time delays.

claim: The disparities between transition times and the responses to them lead to a slight inflation of suppression depth.
source: These disparities between transition times and the responses to them lead to a slight inflation of suppression depth.
evidence: This is an inference about the effect of reaction time delays on the measurement of suppression depth.

claim: Assuming an average reaction time of 500ms, suppression depth will be inflated by ~4.2 dB at the rate of contrast change used in Experiments 1 and 2 (0.07 dB per frame at 60 fps).
source: For example, if we assume an average reaction time of 500ms for appearance and disappearance events, then suppression depth will be inflated by ~4.2 dB at the rate of contrast change used in Experiments 1 and 2 (0.07 dB per frame at 60 fps).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the experimental parameters and assumed reaction time.

claim: The reaction time inflation of ~4.2 dB cannot account for suppression depth in its entirety, which was many times larger at approximately 14 dB across image categories.
source: This cannot account for suppression depth in its entirety, which was many times larger at approximately 14 dB across image categories.
evidence: This is an inference comparing the calculated reaction time effect to the observed suppression depth.

claim: There is no reason to suspect that reaction-times would differ when reporting on the appearance or disappearance of different image categories under CFS.
source: We have no reason to suspect that reaction-times would differ when reporting on the appearance or disappearance of different image categories under CFS, and indeed found no significant evidence for an interaction between thresholds and image categories in our analyses.
evidence: This is supported by the lack of interaction effects in the statistical analyses.

claim: Previous research has attributed faster CFS breakthrough (equivalently, lower contrast) to unconscious processing of suppressed images.
source: Previous research has attributed faster CFS breakthrough (equivalently, lower contrast) to unconscious processing of suppressed images (Gayet et al., 2014; Mudrik et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies making this attribution.

claim: The current study found uniform suppression depth for all tested images, even though bCFS thresholds varied.
source: As the current study found uniform suppression depth for all tested images, even though bCFS thresholds varied, it is clear that differences in bCFS thresholds alone should not be interpreted in terms of expeditious unconscious processing of semantically relevant images.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental findings from Experiments 1 and 2.

claim: Differences in bCFS thresholds alone should not be interpreted in terms of expeditious unconscious processing of semantically relevant images.
source: As the current study found uniform suppression depth for all tested images, even though bCFS thresholds varied, it is clear that differences in bCFS thresholds alone should not be interpreted in terms of expeditious unconscious processing of semantically relevant images.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: If image categories such as faces were processed unconsciously, they reasonably should be harder to re-suppress, and thus have a smaller suppression depth compared to neutral stimuli.
source: Indeed, if image categories such as faces were processed unconsciously, they reasonably should be harder to re-suppress, and thus have a smaller suppression depth compared to neutral stimuli (see Figure 1) – which was not the case.
evidence: This is an inference about what would be expected if unconscious processing occurred, contrasted with the actual findings.

claim: Images with relevant semantic content (here, faces and objects) may break suppression at lower contrasts because they are particularly rich in low-level feature content that promotes image salience.
source: As an alternative to lower bCFS thresholds being due to unconscious processing of images with relevant semantic content, such images (here, faces and objects) may break suppression at lower contrasts because they are particularly rich in low-level feature content that promotes image salience (e.g. Itti and Koch, 2000).
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative explanation, supported by a citation.

claim: Faces and objects could be more salient due to peaks in local image contrast, contour integration, closed curvilinear form, and phase aligned spatial frequency spectra.
source: For example, faces and objects could be more salient due to peaks in local image contrast (Parkhurst and Niebur, 2004), contour integration (Kapadia et al., 2000), closed curvilinear form (concavity: Schmidtmann et al., 2015, and phase aligned spatial frequency spectra Maehara et al., 2009).
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: The combination of low-level image properties plausibly render images such as faces and objects particularly salient within early stages of visual processing and thus lead to lower bCFS thresholds than those measured for less salient stimuli.
source: The combination of these image properties plausibly render images such as faces and objects particularly salient within early stages of visual processing and thus lead to lower bCFS thresholds than those measured for less salient stimuli such as gratings or scrambled noise.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible explanation for the observed differences in bCFS thresholds.

claim: The derivation of salience from low-level image properties is purely stimulus-based and arises without regard to semantic implications.
source: Moreover, this derivation of salience is purely stimulus-based and arises without regard to semantic implications.
evidence: This is an inference about the nature of the proposed salience mechanism.

claim: It is not clear that all variation in bCFS thresholds can be explained by low-level image properties.
source: Some caution is warranted here, however. It is not clear that all variation in bCFS thresholds can be explained by low-level image properties.
evidence: This is speculation about the limitations of the low-level explanation.

claim: There may be important high-level factors that also contribute to the salience of a given target image that make it visible at lower contrasts than other images.
source: There may be important high-level factors that also contribute to the salience of a given target image that make it visible at lower contrasts than other images (Gayet et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2007; Mudrik et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is speculation about possible high-level contributions, supported by citations.

claim: Face images may be salient at lower contrasts than other images such as random noise for high-level reasons specific to face processing.
source: For example, faces provide essential social information and we are very highly attuned to them. Face images may therefore be salient at lower contrasts than other images such as random noise for high-level reasons specific to face processing.
evidence: This is speculation about possible high-level contributions to face salience.

claim: A hybrid-model might be needed for a full account of CFS, similar to those proposed for binocular rivalry.
source: A hybrid-model might therefore be needed for a full account of CFS, similar to those proposed for binocular rivalry (Cao et al., 2021; Wilson, 2003).
evidence: This is speculation about future theoretical developments, supported by citations.

claim: A hybrid model is proposed in which relative suppression depth for a given image arises from low-level interocular mutual inhibition acting equivalently on any kind of image, and the absolute level of breakthrough threshold could be impacted by high-level salience.
source: Based on our results here, we imagine a hybrid model in which relative suppression depth for a given image arises from low-level interocular mutual inhibition acting equivalently on any kind of image (yielding the uniform suppression depth we observe), and the absolute level of breakthrough threshold could be impacted by high-level salience (e.g. Hesse and Tsao, 2020).
evidence: This is speculation about a possible theoretical model based on the experimental findings, supported by a citation.

claim: In Experiment 3, a faster contrast change would reduce the opportunity for adaptation to accrue, thereby requiring a greater change in contrast to overcome suppression during CFS.
source: We predicted that a faster contrast change would reduce the opportunity for adaptation to accrue, thereby requiring a greater change in contrast to overcome suppression during CFS.
evidence: This was a prediction based on theoretical reasoning about adaptation.

claim: In Experiment 3, a slower rate of change should increase the opportunity for adaptation, resulting in reduced suppression depth.
source: Similarly, a slower rate of change should increase the opportunity for adaptation, resulting in the inverse effect.
evidence: This was a prediction based on theoretical reasoning about adaptation.

claim: Strong modulations of suppression depth based on the rate of contrast change were observed in Experiment 3, confirming the predictions.
source: We observed strong modulations of suppression depth based on the rate of contrast change, confirming these predictions (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 3 shown in Figure 4.

claim: In neuroscience, the damped harmonic oscillator (DHO) model provides a valuable mathematical framework for understanding the dynamics of neural systems and their responses to external stimuli, particularly with regard to the interplay between excitation and inhibition.
source: First, in neuroscience, the DHO model provides a valuable mathematical framework for understanding the dynamics of neural systems and their responses to external stimuli, particularly with regard to the interplay between excitation and inhibition (Freeman, 1961; Hodgkin and Huxley, 1952; Spyropoulos et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational neuroscience literature.

claim: In the tCFS context, the high starting contrast of the suprathreshold target is analogous to the external perturbation in the DHO model.
source: In the present context, the high starting contrast of the suprathreshold target in tCFS trials is analogous to the external perturbation.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the experimental paradigm to the DHO model.

claim: The asymptotic differences in thresholds over time are reminiscent of computational models of interocular competition proposing that changes to visual awareness are driven by an out-of-equilibrium cortical network.
source: The asymptotic differences in thresholds over time are reminiscent of both earlier (Wilson, 2003), and more recent computational models Cao et al., 2021 of interocular competition, models proposing that changes to visual awareness are driven by an out-of-equilibrium cortical network.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the experimental findings to existing computational models, supported by citations.

claim: The locus of competing neural ensembles could reside in early visual stages, late stages, or across hierarchical levels of visual processing.
source: We note that the locus of competing neural ensembles could reside in early visual stages (Alais et al., 2010; Lankheet, 2006; Li et al., 2017), late stages (Hohwy et al., 2008) or across hierarchical (Cao et al., 2021; Wilson, 2003) levels of visual processing.
evidence: This is speculation about possible neural mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: Future studies could vary the starting conditions of the tCFS procedure, or manipulate higher-order influences such as attention and expectation to examine whether the return to equilibrium conforms to the predictions of competing models.
source: Although it is beyond the scope of the present work, future studies could vary the starting conditions of the tCFSprocedure, or manipulate higher-order influences such as attention and expectation to examine whether the return to equilibrium we have revealed conforms to the predictions of competing models.
evidence: This is speculation about future research directions.

claim: The tCFS method equips researchers with a convenient method to measure bCFS and reCFS thresholds, and thus suppression depth.
source: The tCFS method equips researchers with a convenient method to measure bCFS and reCFS thresholds, and thus suppression depth.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the methodological contribution of the study.

claim: Using tCFS, a uniform suppression depth exists across image categories.
source: We have used tCFS here to establish that a uniform suppression depth exists across image categories
evidence: This is supported by the experimental findings from Experiments 1 and 2.

claim: Differences in bCFS thresholds alone cannot provide strong evidence for unconscious processing.
source: and that differences in bCFS thresholds alone cannot provide strong evidence for unconscious processing.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The depth of interocular suppression is reported to partially depend on spatial feature similarity between the competing images.
source: For example, the depth of interocular suppression is reported to partially depend on spatial feature similarity between the competing images (Alais and Melcher, 2007; Drewes et al., 2023) and their temporal frequency (Han et al., 2018b; Han and Alais, 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies reporting these effects.

claim: The depth of interocular suppression is reported to partially depend on the temporal frequency of the competing images.
source: For example, the depth of interocular suppression is reported to partially depend on spatial feature similarity between the competing images (Alais and Melcher, 2007; Drewes et al., 2023) and their temporal frequency (Han et al., 2018b; Han and Alais, 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies reporting these effects.

claim: Across three experiments, traditional evidence for unconscious processing based on differences in the threshold to reach awareness (bCFS threshold) provide only half the story.
source: Across three experiments we have introduced the tCFS method and shown that traditional evidence for unconscious processing – based on differences in the threshold to reach awareness (bCFS threshold) – provide only half the story.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Misleading conclusions about unconscious processing must be supported by measures of suppression depth, which can be calculated as the difference between both breakthrough (bCFS) and suppression (reCFS) thresholds.
source: Misleading conclusions about unconscious processing must be supported by measures of suppression depth, which can be calculated as the difference between both breakthrough (bCFS) and suppression (reCFS) thresholds.
evidence: This is an inference about the methodological requirements for studying unconscious processing.

claim: Using the tCFS method, uniform suppression depth was found across five image categories.
source: Using the tCFS method, we have measured these thresholds, and found uniform suppression depth across five image five categories.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental findings from Experiment 2.

claim: Uniform suppression depth is increased with reduced opportunity for target image adaptation, as is the case when target contrast changes rapidly.
source: Notably, this uniform suppression depth is increased with reduced opportunity for target image adaptation, as is the case when target contrast changes rapidly.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental findings from Experiment 3.

claim: The three tCFS experiments refute existing claims of high-level semantic information or target complexity influencing the depth of unconscious processing during interocular suppression.
source: Collectively, the three tCFS experiments refute existing claims of high-level semantic information or target complexity influencing the depth of unconscious processing during interocular suppression.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings across all three experiments.

claim: Future findings may yet confirm differences in suppression depth in certain circumstances, but this will require measurement of both breakthrough and suppression thresholds to demonstrate the requisite changes in suppression depth.
source: Future findings may yet confirm differences in suppression depth in certain circumstances, yet this will require measurement of both breakthrough and suppression thresholds to demonstrate the requisite changes in suppression depth.
evidence: This is speculation about future research possibilities and methodological requirements.

source: A total of 36 undergraduate psychology participants volunteered in exchange for course credit.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the participant sample.

source: All participated with informed consent and had normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the participant characteristics and ethical procedures.

source: Experiment 1: N=20, (15 females), Experiment 2: N=18 (12 females), Experiment 3, N=17 (11 females).

source: All participants in Experiment 3 also did Experiment 2

source: This study was approved by the University of Sydney Human Research Ethics Committee (HREC 2021/048).

source: Visual stimuli were displayed on a Mac Pro (2013; 3.7 GHz Quad-Core Intel Xeon E5) computer, displayed on an Apple LED Cinema monitor (24 inch, 1920x1,200 pixel resolution, 60 Hz refresh rate)

source: All experiments were programmed using custom MATLAB code, and displayed using Matlab (ver R2017b) and Psychtoolbox (ver 3.0.13; Brainard and Vision, 1997).

source: A mirror stereoscope was used to partition participant's vision into separate left- and right-eye views, located approximately 51 cm from the screen, with a total optical path length of 57 cm.

source: Participants dichoptically viewed a high-contrast Mondrian mask pattern (400x400 pixels, 7° x 7°) with one eye and a small target stimulus (130x130 pixels, 2.2° x 2.2°) with the other eye.

source: The Mondrian pattern was greyscale and consisted of overlapping circles of various sizes and intensities and was updated every fifth video frame (12 Hz).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental stimuli.

source: The mask's RMS contrast ranged between 0.07 and 0.09.

claim: Achromatic masks may be optimal to suppress achromatic targets.
source: As previous research has indicated that achromatic masks may be optimal to suppress achromatic targets (reviewed in Pournaghdali and Schwartz, 2020)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: In all experiments, targets were viewed by the right eye and were selected at random from a set that was standardised in RMS contrast (20%) and mean luminance.
source: In all experiments, targets were viewed by the right eye and were selected at random from a set that was standardised in RMS contrast (20%) and mean luminance (before contrast ramping was applied).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental procedure.

claim: Target contrast was ramped up or down by scaling the target image's standard contrast within a range of.02–1.0.
source: Target contrast was ramped up or down by scaling the target image's standard contrast within a range of.02–1.0.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental procedure.

claim: All contrast scaling was done on a logarithmic scale in decibel units to make the changing contrast effectively linear, coinciding with the visual system's logarithmic contrast response function.
source: Importantly, all contrast scaling was done on a logarithmic scale in decibel units (i.e. conDb = 20 x log10(con)) to make the changing contrast effectively linear, thus coinciding with the visual system's logarithmic contrast response function.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental procedure, justified by knowledge of visual system properties.
